opus-5.5.text:
I'd say it was a modest but genuinely useful contribution — mostly in the sense of forcing a conversation that people had been circling around without quite having.

The motivation was that a lot of people in AI safety, myself included, had spent years focused on the question of how we avoid catastrophe in the near term: misalignment, misuse, loss of control. And that's important. But when you ask people, "Okay, suppose we get through that — what does a good world actually look like, stably, once machines can do essentially everything humans can do economically?" you tend to get either a shrug or a fairly hand-wavy answer about abundance and everyone being free to pursue their passions.

What I'd been worried about, and what I wrote about with colleagues under the heading of gradual disempowerment, is that even without any dramatic takeover, the forces that have historically kept institutions roughly aligned with human interests — the fact that states need taxpayers and soldiers, that firms need workers and customers, that culture is produced by and for humans — could quietly erode. If humans stop being necessary, there's not an obvious mechanism keeping the system pointed at us. So the question in the workshop title was meant pretty literally: are there equilibria — stable arrangements, not just nice snapshots — where humans continue to matter?

I think the workshop's main value was in a few things. First, it brought together people from quite different backgrounds — economists, political theorists, alignment researchers, people thinking about governance and institutional design — and made them engage on the same question. A lot of the proposals that sound reasonable within one discipline fall apart pretty quickly when someone from another field asks, "But what keeps that stable? Who enforces it, and why would they keep enforcing it?"

Second, I think it helped raise the bar for what counts as an answer. Saying "we'll have aligned AI that does what we want" just pushes the question back: aligned to whom, and what happens to the competitive dynamics between actors who use AI differently? Saying "we'll have UBI" raises the question of what gives the recipients any bargaining power once their labor is worthless. So we got people to be more precise about the mechanisms.

Where I'd be honest about its limitations: I don't think we came out with a convincing positive vision. If anything, the result was a clearer map of why this is hard, and a sense that many of the comfortable default stories don't hold up. There were some interesting threads — ideas about preserving human-legible institutions, about AI systems that actively help humans coordinate and keep oversight, about deliberately designing in human relevance — but nothing I'd call a solution.

So I'd assess it as a field-building and problem-sharpening exercise. My hope is that it legitimized this as a serious research area rather than something you only talk about late at night, and that more people now feel it's worth working on. Because I think if we wait until we're already in the post-AGI world to figure out what equilibrium we're aiming for, it'll probably be too late to steer toward it.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think the most useful thing the workshop did was make the question legible, rather than answer it. The title was a bit of a provocation. "Are there any good ones?" — and the uncomfortable thing was that when we actually sat down and tried to sketch out futures where humans still matter in some meaningful sense after AGI, most of the pictures people brought either fell apart under scrutiny or quietly assumed the problem away.

So the contribution, if I'm being generous to us, was a kind of negative result. We got a room of economists, political scientists, historians, and AI people together, and the thing we kept running into was that almost every stable arrangement in history has rested on humans being needed for something. Labor, soldiers, taxpayers, voters whose cooperation you have to secure. The reason regimes have had to care about their populations is not mostly that they were nice. It's that they couldn't function otherwise. And once that dependency goes away, a lot of the mechanisms that have kept power accountable just stop having any bite.

What surprised me was how little serious work there was on this. There's an enormous amount of thinking about the transition, about alignment, about avoiding catastrophe in the next few years. There's very little about what the world looks like in the steady state, if we get there. People sort of wave at "post-scarcity" or "universal basic income" as if that resolves it, and the workshop made it pretty clear that it doesn't. A UBI is a policy, and policies are only as durable as the political coalition that maintains them. If the coalition no longer needs you, why does it keep paying?

I'd also say we got some clarity on what the actual axes of disagreement are. Some people thought the answer was to lock in good institutions early, while humans still have leverage. Others thought that was hopeless and that the only real solution is making sure the AI systems themselves genuinely care about human welfare, so that it doesn't depend on incentives at all. And others thought both of those were fine but that the real worry is gradual drift, where no single decision looks bad but you look up fifty years later and humans have no say in anything.

So I wouldn't claim we found a good equilibrium. I'd claim we made it harder to pretend that one is obviously waiting for us. And I think that matters, because a lot of the optimism in this field is really optimism about the transition, and it's just borrowed to cover the destination. The workshop was partly an attempt to call that loan in.

astra-6.text:
I’d distinguish between putting a question on the agenda and answering it. I think the workshop’s contribution was much more the former. We often talk about getting through the transition to AGI, but then there’s this further question: what arrangements would we actually want to persist afterward, and why would they persist?

A desirable future isn’t necessarily a stable one. You might imagine a world where everyone has substantial resources and autonomy, but you still need to ask whether competition, or incentives to accumulate power, would undermine that arrangement. And conversely, an arrangement might be very stable while being pretty undesirable.

So I’d assess the workshop by whether it helped sharpen those questions and expose assumptions in people’s pictures of a good future. I wouldn’t take it as establishing that there’s a particular good equilibrium we know how to reach. The useful step is getting beyond ‘suppose we solve alignment, then things go well’ and asking what else has to be true.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d describe its contribution as exploratory. The title is deliberately a question: if we get very capable AI, are there arrangements we’d actually want to live in that would also be stable? It’s one thing to imagine a lovely future; it’s another to explain why competition or the incentives of powerful actors wouldn’t push us away from it.

The useful distinction is between a desirable outcome and a desirable equilibrium. For any proposed future, you want to ask: who has power, what incentives do they face, and can someone gain by changing the arrangement in a way that makes everyone else worse off?

I wouldn’t claim that a workshop settles those questions. Its contribution is more modest: making the questions explicit, identifying assumptions that need scrutiny, and helping turn vague hopes about life after AGI into proposals we can examine critically.
